Hello everyone I'm curious who is interested in participating on this sub. Please give us aan idea of your scouting background. Also what does scouting/guiding look like in your country? What are your ideas and suggestions for this subverse?

Myself I'm a scout master overseeing and coaching 3 troops in switzerland. Our activities usually take place on saturday afternoon, where we spend time with the kids playing games or learning skills, often in a playful manner. Camps usually take place twice a year. A short one in spring and a longer one during the summer holidays. Although exceptions to that rule beeing rather frequent. Most groups in switzerland are part of the national movement which is a member of both WAGGGS and WOSM. Mixed troops are thus quite widespread. Most troops are secular or only loosly affiliated with a church compared to many other nation's groups. Switzerland is also remarked for the rather young age of it's leaders, often starting by the age of 16 or 17.

I'd like to shape this subverse into a platform where basically all things concering scouting can be discussed. Be it international exchange, learning new people. As well as place to offer and request ideas and advice for activities and projects and other things.

Edit: I'm quite new and unexperienced with modding something like voat. So you you have some know-how and tips or want to lend me a hand please feel free to let me know.

Ingredients:

  • 1 1/4 cups oats, rolled
  • 3/4 cups flour, all-purpose
  • 1/2 cups flour, whole-wheat
  • 1 tablespoon baking powder
  • 1/4 teaspoon salt
  • 3 egg whites
  • 2 1/4 cups buttermilk
  • 2 tablespoon cooking oil
  • 2 tablespoon honey
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  • cooking spray

Directions:

  1. In a large bowl, combine oats, all-purpose flour, whole wheat flour, baking powder, and salt. Make a well in the center of flour mixture; set aside.
  2. In a medium bowl, beat the egg whites with a fork; stir in buttermilk, oil, honey (if desired), and vanilla. Add egg white mixture all at once to flour mixture. Stir just until moistened (batter should be lumpy). Cover batter; allow to stand at room temperature for 15 to 30 minutes.
  3. Coat an unheated griddle or heavy skillet with nonstick cooking spray. Preheat over medium-high heat. For each pancake, pour about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the hot griddle or skillet. Spread batter into a circle about 4 inches in diameter. Cook over medium heat for 4 to 6 minutes or until the pancakes are golden, turning to cook second sides when pancakes have bubbly surfaces and edges are slightly dry.
  4. Garnish with fresh fruit or light syrup, if desired.

Makes 8 servings. Nutrition Information per Serving:

  • Calories: 189
  • Total Fat: 5g
  • Carbohydrates: 28g
  • Fiber: 3g
  • Sugars: 4g
  • Protein: 8g
  • Sodium: 317mg

What is the best way to learn about a area that you just moved to and are unfamiliar with?

Going on foot allows you to get a great sense of the geography and allows you to stop in places easily and get to know people.

However, use your street smarts. I went on a "get to know the area walk" with some friends when I started college. The person leading our group wanted to take us down a few bad side streets. He didn't even realize until I told him that his route choice might end poorly.
Unless there's barb wire fences, and like... a screaming trailer park.
Talk to people! Or walk around, read about it online

I just did this, and I work remotely. I set up in a coffee shop and got to know the employees. Then the owner. Then they introduced me to other people, who introduced me to a few more. I've met builders, artists, entrepreneurs, musicians, software developers, food sustainability coordinators, augmented reality technicians, charcuterie enthusiasts, and mushroom farmers. And that's been in the last week.
Go to a bar. And talk to the locals.

Drive around, go for a walk. Depends on the city. I moved twice in the last 3 years. The first time, I moved to an area that I was already roughly familiar with so I just used landmarks I was familiar with. The second time I moved it was to a very unfamiliar area. I went for a walk, rode my bike, and drove my car around until I was seeing places I was familiar with. I still get lost on the bike path. It's hidden in trees so I get no sense of direction from there.
Pretty obviously you walk or drive around

Geographically? Bike around. In the town where I go to college none of the main roads had bike paths, so I had to figure out how to get around through the side streets. You learn pretty quickly where good restaurants are, where has nice bathrooms, and you get up close and personal with buildings you might just pass by if you were driving

Drive around and listen to music. I don't know if you moved to a driving part of the country or a walking part, but whenever I move somewhere new (which I do a lot) I just get a few albums I've been meaning to listen to, and drive around for a bit. Meet some people your age at the bar, and ride around with them.

Im spending the summer in an entirely new city, in a new state even. I ride/race bikes so I got to explore the surrounding area via bike. And when I was off work and not riding I would just use yelp etc. to find a new coffee shop to walk to or the farmers market on saturdays or some local site to see.

Lots of coffee and walking mostly, its been enjoyable.
